# API-REV-011 canonical authority real publication

## Key findings
- The brief should define one canonical authority for API revision status, semantics, and publication state; mirrors, caches, and generated views must be explicitly subordinate.
- “Real publication” needs an observable transition from draft/review to published, with a durable artifact, timestamp, responsible actor, and immutable revision identifier.
- Authority is credible only if consumers can verify provenance: source location, schema/version, approval decision, and the exact payload or document that was released.
- The workflow should separate content correctness from publication mechanics, while making the handoff between them auditable and repeatable.
- Reviewability improves when the brief includes a small acceptance matrix covering canonical-source selection, conflict handling, publication success, rollback, and post-publication discoverability.

## Risks or open questions
- It is unclear whether “canonical” refers to an API registry, repository, database record, or published document; the brief must name the authority and owner.
- A successful deployment may not equal a successful publication if indexes, consumers, or documentation remain stale.
- Concurrent edits or republishing can create divergent revisions unless idempotency, locking, and supersession rules are explicit.
- Rollback and correction behavior needs definition, especially where already-published identifiers are externally referenced.

## Recommendations or next steps
- State the canonical authority, publication boundary, owner, and non-authoritative mirrors in the opening decision statement.
- Specify a minimal publication record: revision ID, source hash/version, approver, published-at time, status, and discoverable URL or endpoint.
- Add testable acceptance criteria for first publication, repeat publication, conflict rejection, rollback/correction, and consumer verification.
- Require a final reviewer check that the published artifact is the same revision approved in review, not merely a regenerated or cached derivative.

# API-REV-011: Make API revision publication canonical, durable, and verifiable

## Recommendation summary

Adopt one explicitly named canonical authority and owner for API revision status, semantics, and publication state. Treat publication as a durable, observable state transition—not as a side effect of deployment. A revision is published only when the approved payload is recorded with immutable provenance, a publication timestamp, responsible actor, and a discoverable consumer-facing location. Mirrors, caches, registries, and generated documentation remain subordinate and must expose or resolve to the canonical revision rather than compete with it.

## Key evidence

- The authority decision must identify the system of record, accountable owner, publication boundary, and all non-authoritative mirrors.
- A minimal publication record should include immutable revision ID, source hash or version, schema/version, approval decision, approver, published-at timestamp, status, and URL or endpoint.
- The workflow should separate content correctness from publication mechanics while preserving an auditable handoff: the released artifact must be the exact revision approved in review.
- Consumer trust depends on verifiable provenance and discoverability; successful deployment alone does not prove successful publication.
- Acceptance coverage should include canonical-source selection, conflict handling, first publication, repeat publication, rollback/correction, and post-publication consumer verification.

## Risks or cautions

- “Canonical” is ambiguous until the authority type and owner are named; unresolved ambiguity will produce conflicting records.
- Concurrent edits and republishing can create divergent revisions; define idempotency, locking or conflict rejection, and supersession rules.
- Stale indexes, caches, mirrors, or documentation can make a technically successful release appear unpublished.
- Rollback and correction semantics require care when external consumers already reference a published identifier; specify whether identifiers are immutable and how corrections supersede them.

## Next actions

- Choose and document the canonical authority, owner, publication boundary, and mirror policy.
- Define the publication record and provenance verification contract.
- Implement acceptance checks for conflict rejection, repeat publication, rollback/correction, and consumer discoverability.
- Run a reviewer sign-off that compares the published artifact’s revision ID/hash with the approved review record.
